2.title: Is the Letter Really Dead?
2.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The archive nobody is writing

Letter volumes have collapsed. The surprising part is what that has done to the record of ordinary life.

📜✍️
1 · Before you read. The title says an archive is not being written. What do you expect the writer to argue?

Choose one and note what evidence you expect. You will check it against the text.

Text A · What the numbers actually say

Written for this course. Figures from Ofcom, Post Monitoring Report (UK postal regulator).

For most of the last two decades, the story of the letter has been a story of subtraction. Ofcom, the body that regulates post in the United Kingdom, has been counting addressed letters since before the smartphone was ordinary: in 2011 the system carried around 14.3 billion of them, and the figure has since fallen to roughly 6.6 billion. Nothing dramatic has caused this. No government has banned the postage stamp. Volumes have simply been sliding, year after year, at close to nine per cent, and every attempt to reverse the trend has failed.

The obvious explanation is that we have stopped writing, and the obvious explanation is wrong. Thanks to digital media, most of us produce more words before lunch than our great-grandparents wrote in a month. What has changed is not the writing but the surface it lands on. A message arrives — instant, weightless, free — and is read and deleted inside a minute. An email sits in an inbox until somebody clears it. Nothing has waited in an in tray for a fortnight since about 2003.

The postal systems themselves have been adjusting to the arithmetic rather than fighting it. Denmark has given up its guarantee of nationwide letter delivery altogether. In 2025 the British regulator allowed second-class letters to be delivered on alternating weekdays rather than six days a week, because a network built for fourteen billion items cannot be paid for by six. None of these decisions has been popular, and none of them has been reversed. The letter is not being killed off by anyone. It is being quietly priced out of the ordinary week.

Text B · The half of a life that used to be written down

Written for this course.

Historians have been pointing at the consequence for some time. Almost everything we know about ordinary life two centuries ago, we know from correspondence — from letters that nobody at the time thought were important, kept in boxes by people who were not thinking about history at all. For four hundred years that evidence has been quietly accumulating. It has now stopped. A biographer working in 2150 will have millions of public posts to read and almost no private ones, because the confidential half of a life has moved onto servers that are designed to forget.

There is a second loss, and it is harder to measure. A handwritten page carries information that no screen reproduces. You can see where the writer has crossed out a word and chosen a better one, where the handwriting has speeded up towards the end of a difficult sentence, where the pen has pressed too hard. Punctuation does a little of that work in a typed message, and an emoticon does a little more, but neither shows you a person changing their mind in front of you.

None of this has gone unnoticed. Sales of stationery have been climbing in several markets for years, and the shops report that the buyers are not nostalgic pensioners but customers under thirty — people who have never queued for a postage stamp in their lives. Letters have been reappearing wherever slowness is an advantage rather than a fault: in hospitals, in prisons, between grandparents and grandchildren. None of it has rescued the post, and it was never going to. But something has changed all the same. “I’ve been meaning to drop you a line for ages” was once an apology. It has quietly turned into a promise.

2 · Which text does each statement describe? Choose A, B or both.
1It measures a decline with published figures.
2It argues that something valuable is disappearing from the historical record.
3It states that people are writing more than ever.
4It describes decisions taken by postal organisations.
5It accepts that the letter has not been rescued.
6It gives examples of people who are writing letters again.
3 · Choose True or False. None of these is answered word for word in the texts.
1Text A blames the fall in letter volumes on people writing less.
2Text A presents the changes to delivery as a reaction to costs rather than to public demand.
3Text A suggests a single organisation is responsible for the decline.
4Text B implies that future biographers will face a problem their predecessors did not.
5In Text B, the shops’ new customers are people remembering their own letter-writing years.
6Text B treats a letter’s corrections as evidence of the person who wrote it.
7The two texts contradict each other.
8Text B claims that typed punctuation can fully replace what handwriting shows.
4 · Choose the best answer. Two of these depend on what a word refers to.
1In Text A, the figure refers to
2In Text B, It has now stopped means that
3Which sentence is closest in meaning to It is being quietly priced out of the ordinary week?
4Why does Text B call the second loss “harder to measure”?
5What does Text B concede before it makes its final point?
6Taken together, what do the two texts claim has changed?
5 · Complete the summary of both texts. Use one word in each gap.
Since 2011 the volume of addressed in the UK has by more than half, and postal systems have been what they promise rather than fighting the trend. People have not been writing : with we write far more, but a message is read and within a minute. For historians, the loss is the half of a life, which used to be written down. A handwritten page also records the writer’s changes of mind, including every word they . Meanwhile sales of have been climbing among buyers under thirty, and the letter has become a rather than an apology.
6 · Find a word or phrase in the texts that means…
1the process of taking away, of becoming less (Text A)
2moving downwards steadily and without stopping (Text A)
3weighing nothing; costing nothing to carry (Text A)
4a period of two weeks (Text A)
5building up slowly over a long period (Text B)
6copies exactly, so that nothing is lost (Text B)
7going up gradually over time (Text B)
8meant to stay between the sender and the reader (Text B)
7 · Look at the ideas below. Which verb form did the writer use, and why?
1the regulator’s counting, going on across more than a decade
2the drop from 14.3 billion to 6.6 billion
3the postal systems’ response, still going on
4what historians keep saying about the consequence
5the end of four hundred years of gathered evidence
6what has happened to the meaning of “drop you a line”
8 · Write your response to the texts. Answer all three questions.
1Text A says the letter is being priced out rather than killed off. Explain the difference in your own words.
2Text B lists hospitals, prisons and grandparents. What do those three have in common?
3Summarise the combined argument of both texts in three sentences, then say which text you find more convincing and why.

3.title: Reading Between the Lines
3.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The language you can hear across a valley

On one Canary island a whole conversation crosses two kilometres of empty air — and the brain treats it as speech.

🏝️💭
1 · Before you read. Look at the title and the photograph. What kind of place do you expect?

Choose one and note what it would have to do with whistling.

Text A · A language made of whistles

Written for this course, from the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage listing for Silbo Gomero (2009).

Most travellers have never heard of La Gomera, and those who have usually know it for one extraordinary thing. The island is the worn tip of an old volcano, cut through by ravines so deep and slopes so steep that two farms facing each other across a valley can be an hour apart on foot. Long before there were roads, the islanders solved that problem by learning to whistle their language across it.

Silbo Gomero is not a code, and it is not a set of agreed signals for danger or dinner. It consists of a small set of whistled sounds that stand for the vowels and consonants of ordinary Spanish: two whistles carry all five vowels, four more carry the consonants, and the ear separates them by pitch and by whether the sound is continuous or broken. Because the system consists of sounds rather than of ready-made messages, and maps onto the language itself, anything an islander can say, an islander can whistle. A skilled whistler is understood two or three kilometres away, across country that would take most of a morning to cross. At that distance, with the wind moving, visitors regularly mistake it for birdsong.

Nobody is certain where it came from. Most accounts point to North Africa, and when Spanish replaced the older island tongue the whistle was simply adapted to the new language and carried on, as it adapts to any change in the speech around it. It belonged, for ages, to shepherds and to anyone else whose working day was spent on a hillside. It has one built-in weakness: a whistled signal contains far less information than a spoken one, so the same whistle can correspond to several different words. That ambiguity results in genuine mistakes, and whistlers deal with it the way readers deal with a difficult sentence — by repeating, and by relying on context.

Text B · Nearly lost, then legislated back

Written for this course, from the UNESCO listing (2009) and Carreiras, López, Rivero & Corina, Nature 433 (2005).

By the middle of the twentieth century Silbo was in trouble. Roads, telephones and emigration all contributed to its decline, and it acquired a reputation as something rural and backward. Plenty of islanders disapproved of it, and a good number were embarrassed by it: it belonged, they felt, to the poverty their children were escaping. Visitors who had heard of it expected folklore — a ukulele in a hotel lobby, a performance for tourists rather than a working language. By the 1980s the last fluent whistlers were mostly old men.

What rescued it was not enthusiasm but policy. In 1999 the island authorities made Silbo a compulsory subject in every primary and secondary school on La Gomera, and that decision has resulted in something no earlier attempt achieved: a whole generation that grew up whistling in class. In 2009 UNESCO added Silbo Gomero to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, describing it as the only whistled language in the world that is fully developed and practised by a large community — on an island of some 22,000 people.

The most interesting evidence, though, came from a laboratory. In 2005 a team led by Manuel Carreiras published a study in Nature that scanned the brains of fluent whistlers while they listened to Silbo. In those whistlers, the regions that normally handle speech responded to the whistles exactly as they respond to words. In Spanish speakers who could not whistle, the same sounds resulted in nothing of the kind: the brain filed them as noise. Language, it turns out, does not depend on the mouth. It adapts to whatever channel the landscape leaves open.

2 · Which text does each statement describe? Choose A, B or both.
1It explains how the whistling system works.
2It describes an official decision and its consequences.
3It mentions the landscape of the island.
4It reports scientific research.
5It says the origins of the whistle are uncertain.
6It records negative attitudes towards Silbo.
3 · Choose True or False. None of these is answered word for word in the texts.
1Text A says Silbo works by memorising a fixed list of messages.
2The number of separate whistled sounds is smaller than the number of sounds in spoken Spanish.
3Text A treats the ambiguity of the whistle as a problem whistlers work around.
4Opposition to Silbo came mainly from outside the island.
5Text B suggests visitors misunderstood what Silbo was for.
6According to Text B, growing public enthusiasm saved the language.
7In the 2005 study, listeners who could not whistle showed the same brain response as fluent whistlers.
8Taken together, the texts present Silbo as evidence about language in general.
4 · Choose the best answer. Two of these depend on what a word refers to.
1In Text A, that problem refers to
2In Text B, it in “a good number were embarrassed by it” refers to
3Why does Text B mention “a ukulele in a hotel lobby”?
4Which sentence is closest in meaning to “What rescued it was not enthusiasm but policy”?
5What does the 2005 study add that the UNESCO listing does not?
6Which statement would both texts support?
5 · Complete the summary of both texts. Use one word in each gap.
La Gomera is the worn tip of an old cut through by deep , which makes short journeys slow. Silbo Gomero of whistled sounds standing for the vowels and consonants of Spanish, and at a distance it is often mistaken for . Because a whistle carries less information than speech, whistlers rely on repetition and . In the twentieth century, roads, telephones and emigration all to its decline, and many disapproved of it. Making it compulsory at school in 1999 in a whole generation of whistlers, and in 2009 recognised it. A 2005 study found that in fluent whistlers the brain regions used for respond to Silbo, which suggests language can to whatever channel is available.
6 · Find a word or phrase in the texts that means…
1rising or falling very sharply (Text A)
2so unusual that it is hard to believe (Text A)
3how high or low a sound is (Text A)
4a very long time (Text A)
5out of date and unsophisticated (Text B)
6a try, an effort to do something difficult (Text B)
7examined closely with a machine (Text B)
8a route along which a signal travels (Text B)
7 · Complete each idea from the texts with the preposition the writer used, then say what the verb means there.
1Silbo consists a small set of whistled sounds.
2Roads and telephones contributed its decline.
3The whistle was adapted the new language.
4Plenty of islanders disapproved it.
5Most travellers have never heard La Gomera.
6The 1999 decision has resulted a generation of whistlers.
8 · Write your response to the texts. Answer all three questions.
1Text B says Silbo was saved by policy rather than enthusiasm. Is a compulsory school subject a real rescue, or does it turn a language into a museum piece?
2Explain in your own words why the 2005 study matters more than a count of how many people whistle.
3Summarise the combined argument of both texts in three sentences, then say what the evidence does not prove.

6.title: Rules at Work
6.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The rules nobody explains

Four strange workplace rules, and what a careful reader can work out about each of them.

💼🔍
1 · Before you read. Look at the title. Why do you think companies leave rules unexplained?

Choose one and note which kind of company it would apply to. You will check it against the texts.

Text A · Four rules, no reasons

Written for this course.

Every organisation has at least one rule that nobody on the staff can account for. A German manufacturer insists on drivers reversing into every space in the car park. A firm in Osaka does not allow anybody to leave the building during the lunch break. A London agency once told its people that personal calls made at a desk would count against them at the annual review. A Rotterdam warehouse requires two signatures on a form that only one person ever reads. None of the four ever explained why, and in three of them the rule still applies to visitors as well as to employees.

The Osaka rule resists the obvious explanation. It can’t have been about laziness, since the same staff regularly work late without being asked twice. It might have been about the telephones, which somebody has to answer at one o’clock, or it could have been a way of protecting the younger employees from being sent out on errands during the only hour that belongs to them. Both readings fit the evidence; neither can be confirmed, and the company has never justified the working practice in writing.

The London rule is the easiest to reconstruct and the least flattering. Somebody must have complained about one particular colleague. The agency can’t have wanted to accuse that person openly, because a direct conversation would have identified the complainant as well. Writing a rule that applies to everybody was simpler than choosing to criticize one person for it, and it allowed the management to blame nobody in public while making the point in private. It may not have been fair, but it worked, and nobody in the office could have proved who it was aimed at.

Text B · Reading a rule backwards

Written for this course. Parking guidance from the UK Health and Safety Executive, Workplace Transport Safety.

Turn a rule round and it becomes readable. The German parking rule must have begun as a safety measure rather than a matter of neatness. Britain’s Health and Safety Executive advises that where a site cannot be laid out for drive-through parking, the arrangements should encourage reverse parking, precisely because reversing out into a flow of moving traffic is where the collisions happen. Somebody at that plant may well have read the same guidance. The rule can’t have been invented to make the yard look tidy: a company that only wanted tidiness would not have troubled to enforce it on visitors.

The legal background makes the reasoning tighter. An employer who exposes staff to a risk that could reasonably have been designed out can face harsh penalties, and where the failure is serious enough a manager may be given a suspended sentence rather than a fine. Read in that light, a rule that looks petty starts to look expensive. Nobody wrote it in order to irritate the workforce; somebody wrote it with a lawyer in the room, and the lawyer must have been thinking about what a court would say afterwards.

What unexplained rules have in common is that each one is an answer to a question nobody wrote down. Regulations at work are the residue of incidents, and the incident is almost never recorded beside the regulation it produced. You can’t count on the reason surviving; you can only reconstruct it from the shape of what is left, the way an archaeologist reconstructs a building from the holes its posts left in the ground. The reconstruction is worth doing, because the alternative — assuming that the rule must have been designed to annoy you — is usually wrong, and it is always the least interesting explanation available. Whoever wrote the rule could have added one sentence of explanation, and must have decided, for reasons of their own, not to.

2 · Which text does each statement describe? Choose A, B or both.
1It lists rules without interpreting them.
2It refers to official safety guidance.
3It reconstructs the reason behind a rule.
4It explains what happens legally when an employer creates avoidable risk.
5It describes a rule written about one person but addressed to everybody.
6It states a general method for interpreting rules.
3 · Choose True or False. None of these is answered word for word in the texts.

2Text A is confident about which explanation of the Osaka rule is correct.
3The Osaka rule is presented as inconsistent with how those employees behave at other times.
4Text A says the office eventually found out who the London rule was written for.
5Text B treats the enforcement of the parking rule on visitors as evidence about its purpose.
6The Health and Safety Executive recommends reverse parking in every workplace car park.
7Text B states as fact that the German company read the official guidance.
8Text B argues that most workplace rules are written deliberately to control people.
4 · Choose the best answer. Two of these depend on what a word refers to.
1In Text B, Turn a rule round means
2In Text A, it in “it allowed the management to blame nobody in public” refers to
3Which sentence is closest in meaning to “a rule that looks petty starts to look expensive”?
4Why does Text B compare the reader to an archaeologist?
5What does Text B add that Text A does not?
6Which statement would both texts support?
5 · Complete the summary of both texts. Use one word in each gap.
Four employers enforce rules that no member of can explain. The German car-park rule must have started as a measure, since official guidance encourages reverse parking where reversing out into traffic would otherwise be necessary. An employer who staff to an avoidable risk can face harsh , and in serious cases a manager may receive a suspended . The Osaka lunch-break rule can’t have been about laziness, and the company has never the working practice in writing. The London agency wrote a rule for everybody because it did not want to one person openly, and that allowed it to nobody in public. Text B concludes that you cannot on the reason surviving, and that assuming a rule was written to you is usually wrong.
6 · Find a word or phrase in the texts that means…
1explain or give a reason for (Text A)
2short journeys made to collect or deliver something (Text A)
3the person who made the original complaint (Text A)
4being tidy and well arranged (Text B)
5small and unimportant, in a way that seems mean (Text B)
6to annoy somebody slightly but repeatedly (Text B)
7what is left behind after the rest has gone (Text B)
8all the people employed by an organisation (Text B)
7 · Look at the ideas below. Which form did the writer use, and how certain is it?
1the origin of the parking rule — the writer is confident
2the German company reading the guidance — likely, but unproven
3tidiness as the reason for the parking rule — the writer rejects it
4the telephones as the reason for the Osaka rule — one option of two
5the complaint behind the London rule — treated as certain
6the agency’s willingness to name the person — ruled out
8 · Write your response to the texts. Answer all three questions.
1The Rotterdam rule — two signatures on a form only one person reads — is never explained. Write what must have happened, and what can’t have.
2Explain in your own words why Text B says a petty-looking rule can be expensive.
3Describe one rule from a place you have worked or studied, then work out what must have caused it and what can be ruled out.

7.title: Reading Without All the Words
7.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

Four days before the bicentenary

Three volunteers, one museum, and a set of messages with half the words missing.

🏛️📱
1 · Before you read. Look at the title and the first line below. Who do you think is writing to whom?
The first line

Been here since eight. Nothing in the hall yet.

Choose one and note what in the line told you. You will check it against the texts.

Text A · The morning thread

Written for this course. Messages between three museum volunteers.

Priya, 08.14 — Been here since eight. Nothing in the hall yet. Banners still in boxes. Multicoloured ones for the courtyard, plain for inside — don’t mix them up.

Dan, 08.31 — On my way. Stuck on the ring road. Any sign of the bilingual signs? Ordered them in March, never came. Rang twice. No answer either time.

Priya, 08.33 — Arrived Friday. In the office, under the box of programmes. Sam’s doing the chairs — semicircle in front of the monoplane, not rows. Looks better and holds more.

Sam, 09.02 — Morning both. Chairs done. Two rooms interconnect now the builders have gone, so people can walk straight through instead of going back round. Much better for the tour.

Priya, 09.10 — Good. Programmes here too. Two hundred years of this place, and the first batch came back with the date wrong. Reprinting. Cost me an afternoon.

Sam, 09.14 — How many wrong? All of them, or just the first box?

Dan, 09.40 — Here at last. Parked behind the delivery bay. Illegal, I know. Ten minutes, no more.

Priya, 09.44 — Move it. Warden was round twice yesterday. Fined one of the caterers’ drivers. Forty pounds, apparently.

Dan, 10.31 — Catering confirmed. Sixty for the reception, forty for the talk. Tea urns from the church again. Ours still broken since March.

Priya, 10.36 — Fine. Guest book on the desk by the door, not by the monoplane. People stop to write and block the doorway.

Sam, 10.15 — Question. The figurehead — the semi-human one from the wreck — hall or side room? Was in the hall last time. Bit dark in there now, though.

Priya, 10.18 — Hall. Everyone photographs it. Side room’s for the biannual newsletter display and the old photographs. Lights fixed on Monday anyway.

Text B · Midday, and the note on the door

Written for this course. The same thread later, a note pinned to a door, and an email.

Dan, 11.02 — Bad news. Speaker’s flight delayed. Intercontinental, so nothing before tomorrow evening now. Not tonight.

Sam, 11.05 — Which speaker? The semi-retired professor, or the one who pays for everything?

Dan, 11.07 — The professor. The multimillionaire’s driving up. Arrives Thursday, wants an hour in the hall first.

Priya, 11.12 — Fine. Professor first, donor second. Keep the professor short — lovely man, but speaks in a monotone and nobody lasts twenty minutes.

Priya, 11.31 — One more thing. Donor wants a photograph with the monoplane. Not with the sandwiches. Make sure somebody’s watching.

Sam, 11.20 — Ladder found. Behind the boiler, of course. Bulbs next.

Dan, 15.02 — Van driver rang back. Six banners still in the depot. Says Thursday morning. Chasing him again at eight.

Sam, 17.12 — Bulbs done, side room usable. Left the ladder by the stairs. Someone move it before Thursday, please.

Priya, 17.44 — Programmes reprinted, correct date, bicentenary logo on the cover. Two boxes in the office, one in the hall. Don’t open the hall box till Thursday morning, and keep it away from the caterers.

Pinned to the office door, 16.40 — Gone to the printer’s. Back by six. Banners counted — forty-two. Should be forty-eight. Six missing, probably still in the van, unless the driver unloaded them somewhere else. Don’t move the chairs. P.

Email, 21.55. From Priya. Subject: Bicentenary, Thursday — Dan, Sam — quick summary before I forget. Signs: found, in the office. Chairs: done, semicircle, please leave them. Figurehead: hall, not side room. Speaker: delayed, so Thursday not Wednesday. Banners: six short, chasing the driver in the morning. Anything I’ve missed, tell me tonight rather than at eight on Thursday. P.

2 · Which text does each statement describe? Choose A, B or both.
1It settles where an exhibit will stand.
2It reports a change to the timetable.
3It contains an instruction about the chairs.
4It mentions a parking problem.
5It records a number that does not add up.
6It refers to the monoplane.
3 · Choose True or False. You will have to supply the words the writers left out.
1In Text A, Dan telephoned about the signs on more than one occasion.
2The bilingual signs never reached the museum.
3The multicoloured banners are meant for indoor use.
4The two interconnecting rooms improve how visitors move around.
5The person who was fined worked for the museum.
6The lighting in the side room is a permanent problem.
7In Text B, the professor and the donor are travelling by different means.
8Priya’s email introduces a decision that had not been taken during the day.
4 · Choose the best answer. Each of these depends on something the writer did not say.
1In Text A, Arrived Friday refers to
2In Text A, Ten minutes, no more means
3In Text A, Move it is best understood as
4In Text B, Sam’s question at 11.05 shows that
5Why does Priya write “Not with the sandwiches”?

Sam has arranged the chairs in a in front of the , and two rooms now , so visitors can walk straight through. Dan parks behind the delivery bay and is told to move. The figurehead will go in the hall. In Text B the professor’s flight is delayed, so he will speak on Thursday, and Priya warns that he speaks in a and should be kept short.

9.title: Out of Your Comfort Zone
9.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The week I stopped being sensible

A first-person account of fourteen days that did not go to plan.

🏔🌿
1 · Before you read. The writer calls herself “sensible”, not “boring”. What does that choice of word suggest?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · Fourteen days I had not agreed to

Written for this course.

Until two years ago I had never slept anywhere without a lock on the door. I was not an adventurous person and I had never pretended to be one. My holidays were cities, museums and a return flight booked before I left. Then my sister paid for a fourteen-day trek through a remote valley in the north, told me afterwards, and refused to discuss it. Her argument was that I needed to step out of my comfort zone. Mine was that I had a job, a cat and no boots.

By the end of the first afternoon I had already stopped speaking. We had been walking for six hours, my bag weighed more than I had estimated, and the physical side of it was worse than anything I had prepared for. Nobody had warned me that the difficulty of a trek is not the distance but the small decisions: whether to stop now or in twenty minutes, whether the pain in your heel is a blister or the boot. My sister, who had done this sort of thing before, made a poor companion that first day. She kept pointing out that the views were stunning, which they were, and which did not help.

The trip turned on day four. We had lost the path an hour earlier and had been arguing about the map when an old man appeared from nowhere with two dogs. Neither of us spoke his language and he had no interest in ours. He looked at the map, laughed at it, and walked us to the col. There he pointed at our destination, a white village on the far side of the valley, and went home. The whole encounter lasted less than an hour and it is the only part of the fortnight I would call remarkable. Neither of us had done anything to deserve it.

Text B · What it was not

Written for this course.

What surprised me afterwards was how little of it was about courage. I finished the walk because turning back had become more trouble than going on, and that is not the same thing. There was no moment on any of the fourteen days when I chose the difficult option over the easy one; there was simply never an easy one available. People who describe a trek as a feat, or who come home calling themselves explorers, have usually skipped that part of the story. Nobody had sent us on a mission. We were two women with a map neither of us could read.

Something did change, though, and it changed later than I expected. By the second week I had taken over the route, the food and the timing, not out of determination but because my sister had stopped doing it and somebody had to. I was carrying a responsibility I had spent forty years arranging my life to avoid, and it turned out to weigh about as much as the bag. On the last evening I wandered round a town I had never heard of, alone, in the dark, for two hours, and enjoyed every minute of it.

I am not a different person. I still book the return flight first, and I have not thrown away the lock on the door. But I am determined to go back, and this time I have booked it myself, which my sister says proves her point and which I am not going to admit. If she had asked me first, I would have said no, and I would have been wrong; I am prepared to accept that much and no more.

2 · Which text does each statement describe? Choose A, B or both.
1It describes how the trip was arranged.
2It rejects a word other people would use about the trip.
3It reports an act of kindness from a stranger.

10.title: An Extraordinary Escape
10.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The box that arrived in Philadelphia

Twenty-seven hours, three states, and four men waiting in an office for a crate marked “dry goods”.

📦🔒
1 · Before you read. The crate was labelled “dry goods” and “this side up”. What does the second label tell you?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · Twenty-seven hours

Written for this course, from Encyclopedia Virginia and the Pennsylvania Center for the Book.

By six o’clock on the morning of 24 March 1849, four men in a Philadelphia office had already been waiting for two hours. They had been told to expect a wooden crate from Richmond, in Virginia, labelled as dry goods. They had not been told what to do if it arrived closed and silent. All four were tense. When the wagon finally came in from a muddy yard, the driver, who had been given no explanation at all, looked puzzled at how many people had gathered for one box.

Inside was Henry Brown, who had been born into slavery in Louisa County, Virginia, around 1815, and who had been sent at fifteen to a tobacco factory in Richmond. He had been treated less harshly than many; he had married, and he had been paying his wife’s owner, out of his own wages, not to sell her. In 1848 she and their three children were sold to a buyer in another state anyway. Brown was furious, and then, for months, simply miserable. Every promise had turned out to be worth nothing, and the bitter clarity that followed decided what he did next.

The journey took twenty-seven hours, using almost every kind of transport then available: wagon, railway, steamboat, ferry, wagon again. For several of those hours the box had been left upside down, and Brown, who could not move and could not call out, later wrote that he had felt the blood forcing itself into his head and had been certain he was dying. He had been given a little water and a few biscuits, and nothing else. Petrified of making a sound, he had lain still throughout. At least twice, anxious handlers who were puzzled by the weight had come close to opening it. When the lid finally came off he was disorientated and could not stand. The men, who had been terrified that they had waited too long, were enormously relieved, and then delighted.

Text B · What the story cost

Written for this course, from the Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on Henry ‘Box’ Brown and the Pennsylvania Center for the Book.

The plan had been Brown’s own. Through James C. A. Smith, a free Black man who sang in the same church choir, he had reached Samuel A. Smith, a white shoemaker who agreed to help for a fee. Brown had saved 166 dollars and handed over 86 of them. A carpenter had built the crate to order: roughly three feet long, two and a half deep, two wide, with holes bored for air. It was consigned to the Adams Express Company, which had built a reputation for asking no questions, and addressed to James Miller McKim of the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society. Letters had been exchanged for weeks beforehand to ensure that somebody would be in the office when it came.

Within weeks of his arrival Brown had become a speaker on the anti-slavery circuit; at a convention in New England he was introduced by the nickname that stayed with him, and by September a narrative of the escape had been published. Not everybody approved. Frederick Douglass was upset that the method had been described in print at all, since printing it had closed the route for anybody who might have used it afterwards.

The warning was justified. When Samuel Smith tried to send others north the same way later that year, he was arrested and sentenced to years in the Virginia penitentiary. Brown himself left for England after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, toured for years with a huge moving panorama of scenes from slavery, and ended his working life on stage as a magician. Historians have since investigated the route, the dates and the paperwork in detail. But his legacy is not really the box. It is what he did with the story once he was out of it.

13.title: Crossing Cultures
13.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The longest night in Lerwick

One town, one Tuesday in January, and a boat built in order to be burned.

🔥⛵
1 · Before you read. A town builds a wooden ship every winter and destroys it in one evening. What would you expect the reason to be?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · A ceremony assembled in stages

Written for this course, from the Lerwick Up Helly Aa Committee’s own history of the festival.

On the last Tuesday in January, the town of Lerwick in Shetland burns a boat. The galley is a replica longship, built over about four months by people who will stand and watch it destroyed. At half past seven a rocket goes up, a thousand torches are lit, and the procession moves off through a crowd of five thousand or more. By ten in the evening there is nothing left of the winter’s work but ash.

The Norse history behind all this is perfectly real. The islands were settled from Norway more than a thousand years ago; a form of Norse was spoken here for centuries afterwards, and the settlers left their names on almost every hill. Plenty of families can find ancestors in the parish records, and the descendants of those families still work the same ground. What is a great deal younger than the costumes suggest is the festival itself.

Up Helly Aa grew out of tar barrelling, a rough midwinter custom in which squads of young men dragged barrels of burning tar through the streets on sledges, making trouble. Around 1870 a group of young men in the town replaced it with something better organised: a later date, elaborate disguise, and a torchlit parade. The Viking element arrived afterwards, in stages. A first sign of it appears in 1877; the galley itself only in the late 1880s; the title Guizer Jarl, worn by the chief guizer, not until 1906; and a Viking squad in the procession every single year only after the First World War. The ceremony people describe as ancient was established, piece by piece, by Victorians who admired a past they had never seen.

Text B · Whose night is it?

Written for this course, from reporting by the BBC and Shetland.org.

None of that makes the festival false. A custom does not have to be old to be genuine; it has to be carried by a community that pays for it, builds it and turns up to it in the rain. Ancestry is not the qualification either. In practice a squad is formed among people who live in the town now — an immigrant of ten years’ standing can carry a torch, and a citizen by descent who moved to Aberdeen in 1998 cannot.

Living customs also argue with themselves. For roughly 142 years the Lerwick squads were open to men only; women organised the halls, the food and the all-night parties, and a good many of them defended that division firmly. Smaller fire festivals elsewhere in Shetland had female participants far earlier, and one of them appointed a woman as its Jarl in 2015. After a two-year gap caused by the pandemic, the Lerwick committee removed the restriction from the 2023 festival, and the following year the Jarl’s own squad included his daughter and three of his nieces. A tradition that can be amended is not a weaker tradition. It is a working one.

The other pressure comes from outside. The burning galley is the feature every camera wants, and the procession is now streamed live, which has made a town of seven thousand people known globally. The community has had to decide, more than once, how much of the night belongs to the visitors. So far the answer has been roughly this: the fire is yours to look at, and the twenty-four hours in the halls afterwards, which is where the festival actually lives, are ours.

14.title: Alone or Together?
14.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The house with no spare bedroom

An article on shared living, and on what a community does with the rooms nobody uses.

🛌🌱
1 · Before you read. Which of these would you find hardest to share with your neighbours?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · The room used nine nights a year

Written for this course, from the UK Cohousing Network and published research on Danish cohousing.

Most of the houses built in Europe over the last century contain a room that is used for about nine nights a year. A few families use the spare bedroom more than that; hardly any use it enough to justify heating it, cleaning it and paying a mortgage on it. Multiply that by every household in a neighbourhood and the waste stops looking like a private eccentricity and starts looking like a planning problem.

Co-housing starts from exactly this observation. Each family owns or rents a private property, with its own kitchen and its own front door, and every resident can shut that door on the rest of the world. What the households do not each own is a guest room, a laundry, a workshop or an entertainment space. There is one of each, shared, and both the cost and the cleaning are divided among all of them. The private dwellings are usually smaller than average on purpose, because the money saved goes into the common house instead.

Neither the idea nor the arithmetic is new. The first modern scheme opened north of Copenhagen in 1972, after its architect’s earlier attempt had collapsed in the face of neighbours’ objections; twenty-seven households moved in, and a second Danish project followed a year later. Several hundred communities now exist across northern Europe, and the Netherlands alone has more than three hundred. Most of them were designed by the people who were going to live in them, which is slow, and which is also the point: residents who have argued for two years about where to put the bins tend to know their neighbours.

Text B · What the research actually finds

Written for this course, from Choi, European Planning Studies (2004) and comparative studies of senior cohousing in Denmark and the Netherlands.

What has changed is who applies. Most of the early residents were young families looking for somewhere the children could be watched by more than two adults. A large number of applicants now are people over seventy who want to go on living independently, in a property they control, and who know perfectly well what the alternative looks like. Studies of senior schemes in Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands report the same finding: the dominant motive is not practical help but the avoidance of isolation. Several of them also record higher levels of social and physical activity among residents than among comparable people living alone.

None of this suits everybody, and the literature is honest about that. Some of the meetings are long, and a few of them are about washing machines. Decisions taken by consensus can take months. Residents eat separately most nights, and plenty of them say the shared meals are the part they would give up first. Cohousing also tends to attract people with time, confidence and a university education, which limits how far it can be offered as a general answer to anything.

But almost all of them mention the same thing, and it is not the guest room. Somebody notices when your curtains stay shut. In a period that has seen a steady rise in one-person households across Europe, and growth in the number of people studying and working at home through distance learning, that is not a small claim. The spare bedroom was never really the problem. It was the clearest sign of a way of building that assumed everyone would rather be left alone.

18.title: Best Ways to Invest Your Time
18.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

What you will have done with the time

Most people plan their money forty years ahead and their free time about forty minutes ahead.

⏳💰
1 · Before you read. Imagine you were given six free hours every day, for the rest of your life. How would that feel after a month?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · The fund nobody manages

Written for this course, using life-expectancy and time-use arithmetic from the American Time Use Survey.

Ask somebody where their money will be in thirty years and they will usually have an answer. There will be a pension, possibly an inheritance, some vague expectation about healthcare costs, and a figure they have looked up more than once. Ask the same person how they will be spending their Tuesday evenings in 2055 and the question sounds absurd. We think ahead about money as a matter of course. We take time for granted, and by the time we notice, we will already have spent most of it.

The arithmetic is not complicated. If you are thirty now, you will have lived roughly eleven thousand days and, on current life expectancy in most of Europe, you will live perhaps another nineteen thousand. Subtract sleep and work and the commute, and the discretionary hours — the ones nobody else has a claim on — come to something in the region of four a day. By the time you are seventy you will have accumulated more than fifty thousand of them. By then you will also have been working for something like forty-five years, and you will still not have decided what the evenings are for. That is a larger fund than most people’s savings, and almost nobody manages it.

People who throw their money around are considered foolish; people who throw their hours around are considered normal, and the only real difference is that nobody sends you a statement. A bank will tell you what you spent last month and what it left you with. Nothing performs that service for a Sunday afternoon. Next Sunday will be disappearing in exactly the same way, and by Monday you will have forgotten what happened to it. This is why the hours disappear without an argument: not because anyone decides to waste them, but because nothing in the system makes the loss visible while there is still time to do something about it.

Text B · The two-to-five-hour finding

Written for this course, from Sharif, Mogilner & Hershfield, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 121(4), 2021.

The obvious conclusion is that more free time must be better, and the research says otherwise. In 2021 three researchers at Wharton and UCLA examined responses from more than 35,000 Americans, most drawn from the American Time Use Survey, plus two experiments of their own. Well-being rose as daily discretionary time increased, levelled off after about two hours, and then began to fall again beyond roughly five. Too little time produces stress. Too much, the authors argue, produces something else: a lacking sense of productivity and purpose. Most readers will be living somewhere inside that curve.

Almost everyone will have met that finding by the time they stop working. Anyone who retires at sixty-five will be handling eight or nine unstructured hours a day, every day, for perhaps twenty years. By the end of the first decade they will have spent more waking hours in retirement than in the whole of secondary school and university combined. The people who cope best, according to the same research, are not those with the most flexibility but those whose extra hours go into something worthwhile — and time with others counts. By seventy-five they will have made that decision some three thousand times.

The practical advice that follows is duller than it sounds. Do not while away the hours waiting for a better use to appear; it will not. Do not kill time and call it resting, because the two feel quite different afterwards. Take your time over things that repay it, and put a limit on the things that do not. Above all, stay in contact: the friendships people lose are almost never ended deliberately, and once you have lost touch with somebody for five years you will usually have lost them for good, while still meaning to call. In twenty years you will not be remembering the evenings you filled efficiently, but whether you made the most of the ones that mattered.

19.title: Skimming for the Main Idea
19.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

Can anybody really read four times faster?

A text with one clear idea per paragraph — about why that is the only thing that makes fast reading possible.

👀📖
1 · Before you read. How fast do you think an average adult reads a non-fiction text in their own language?

Choose one and note it. You will check it against paragraph 1.

Text A · Why the eyes are not the problem

Written for this course, from Rayner et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest 17(1), 2016, and Brysbaert’s meta-analysis of adult reading rates.

Most adults read far more slowly than they believe they do. A review of 190 studies covering more than eighteen thousand participants put the average silent reading rate for adults in English at around 238 words a minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction. Ask people to estimate their own rate and they overestimate it, sometimes by a factor of two. The gap between what people do and what they think they do is the first thing any honest discussion of speed has to deal with. Careful measurement of reading speed is old and well established, which is part of what makes the claims of the speed-reading industry so easy to test.

The real limit is not the eyes. It is tempting to assume that a proficient reader is simply one whose eyes move efficiently, but the movement of the eyes accounts for no more than about a tenth of the total time spent reading. The rest goes on recognising each word and working out how the words combine. That is a language problem, not an optical one, and no training can make it disappear.

Speed-reading programmes generally work by removing something that turns out to be useful. The industry is not new — Evelyn Wood launched her training programme in 1959 — but it now includes a multitude of apps that flash single words on a screen so that the reader cannot look back. Looking back is exactly the problem. Skilled readers constantly make reference to words they have already passed, and most of those backward movements exist to repair a misunderstanding. Prevent them and the misunderstanding simply stays where it is.

Text B · What is left, once the promises are removed

Written for this course, from Rayner et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest 17(1), 2016.

The evidence on trained speed readers points consistently in one direction. Studies of people who have completed such courses find that the increase in speed comes with a reduction in comprehension; the achievement is real, but it is not the achievement advertised. Investigations of the most impressive performers usually reveal something simpler: they already knew a great deal about the subject. Without that prior knowledge, the same readers cannot answer substantive questions about what they have supposedly read.

Skimming, however, is a genuine skill and a defensible one. If a full understanding is not the goal, a reader can move through a text much faster and come away with moderate comprehension — enough to judge relevance, locate specific information, and decide whether the piece deserves a proper reading. Skimmers do this by reading headings, first sentences and key words, which is why the significance of a well-built paragraph is practical rather than decorative. Given the scarcity of attention most readers are working with, a paragraph that announces its own subject in its first line lets them get on with the argument instead of hunting for it.

The only reliable route to reading faster is unglamorous. The more often a reader has met a word, the more quickly it is processed, so wider reading and a larger vocabulary yield modest but genuine and measurable gains over time. This is slower than any course promises, which is presumably why people drop out of the courses and give up on the apps. It amounts to advice nobody wants: read more, look words up, and do your best with a text before deciding it is too hard.

21.title: Dark Days and White Nights
21.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

Sixty days without a sunrise

Two months of polar night at 69° north — and the research on why it is not what visitors expect.

🌑❄️
1 · Before you read. Two months without a sunrise. What would you expect the effect on people to be?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · What two months of night are actually like

Written for this course.

The first thing anybody asks, once they hear where I live, is how I cope with the dark. Tromsø sits at just over sixty-nine degrees north, well above the Arctic Circle, and for about two months the sun never climbs above the horizon at all. People automatically assume that those weeks must be miserable. They are not. They are the part of the year I would keep if somebody made me choose.

The cause is not the weather but the tilt of the Earth’s axis, which is basically twenty-three and a half degrees and which everybody learns at school and nobody believes until they have lived through it. Above a certain line the polar night simply arrives. During the darkest weeks the town gets two or three hours of indirect light, thrown up into the sky from a sun that is still below the ridge. The sky turns deep blue late in the morning, grows slightly lighter for an hour, and then closes again. Winters in my homeland are considerably shorter and dramatic in a different way: bitterly cold, brutally bright, and finished by March.

What surprises visitors most is how rarely anybody stays indoors. Children are outside at nine in the morning, dressed extremely warmly, playing under artificial light on the school field. The ski track on the mountainside above the town is lit from end to end, and it is used far more heavily in December than in April. Houses are lit softly too, with a candle in almost every window, which sounds sentimental and is basically practical: it makes a street feel cosy rather than closed.

Text B · What the research says about it

Written for this course, from Johnsen, Wynn & Bratlid, BMC Psychiatry 12:225 (2012), and Leibowitz & Vittersø’s work on wintertime mindset at the University of Tromsø.

The research is more interesting than the postcard. A large population study published in 2012, covering nearly nine thousand adults in Tromsø, found no significant seasonal difference in mental distress at all — but it did find that sleeping problems were significantly more common in winter than in any other season. That is a careful result rather than a cheerful one. The darkness appears to cost people their sleep without costing them their mood, which is not the story either the optimists or the pessimists usually tell.

Why the mood holds up is a separate question, and one answer points at expectation. A health psychologist who spent ten months in the town, working with a colleague at the university there, built a short questionnaire measuring whether residents saw winter as something to be enjoyed or something to be endured. People who scored highly on it — who agreed that there was a great deal to enjoy in the season — reported greater life satisfaction and more positive emotion. The contrast with how the same months are described further south is striking, and it is cultural before it is biological.

Then, gradually, it comes back. On the morning the sun first appears above the ridge, the whole town behaves slightly oddly and extremely happily; people stand on the harbour wall and watch for the twenty minutes it lasts. Six months later the opposite arrives, and it is not automatically easier. By June it never really gets dark, which is magical for a week and mildly irritating for the two months afterwards. Nobody who has not lived through both seasons quite believes that the light one can be the harder of the two.

23.title: Same Meaning, Different Word
23.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

Believing in the moon

A text that keeps pointing backwards at itself — and a belief that thirty-seven studies could not remove.

🌕🧠
1 · Before you read. Do nurses, police officers and teachers notice more difficult behaviour at full moon?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · What the counting showed

Written for this course, from Rotton & Kelly, Psychological Bulletin 97(2), 1985.

Ask ten people whether a full moon changes the way we behave, and most of them will say that it does. This is one of the most widespread beliefs in the world, and it survives in the absence of any supporting evidence at all. Nurses repeat it; so do police officers, and some of them will tell you that they can feel the difference on a busy night. That feeling is genuine. The pattern behind it is not.

The checking has been done, and it was done thoroughly. In 1985 two researchers collected thirty-seven published and unpublished studies of the supposed effect and combined them statistically, looking at hospital admissions, crisis calls, homicides and other criminal offences. A few individual results reached statistical significance; almost any large collection of studies will retain one or two of those. But when the whole set was measured together, the phase of the moon accounted for no more than one per cent of the variation in the behaviour usually described as lunacy. The authors advised that further work on the question was unnecessary. Forty years later, the belief is exactly where it was.

The reason it survives is not complicated. We notice the nights that fit the story and forget the ones that do not. A ward that is unusually lively during a full moon confirms the belief; a quiet one does nothing to it, because nobody retains a quiet Tuesday. Neither praise for the careful studies nor criticism of the sloppy ones has changed a single mind, and it is easy to see why: the belief was never built out of counted evidence in the first place, so counted evidence cannot take it apart.

Text B · The same shape, in other stories

Written for this course.

Something similar happens with the physical explanation people offer. The moon moves the tides, they say, and we are mostly water, so it must move us as well. This sounds reasonable and is not. Tides are produced by the difference in pull across an entire ocean; on a body the size of a person that difference is smaller than the weight of a drop of sweat. The argument feels scientific because it uses the right vocabulary. That is a different thing from being correct.

Other beliefs of this kind are stranger. Millions of people are convinced that the 1969 landings were faked, and those who think so usually begin with the same detail: the flag appears to move, and there is no wind up there to make it do so. The explanation is accidental rather than deliberate. The pole was being twisted as it was pushed into the ground, and in the presence of no air to slow the motion, the movement simply continued for longer than it would here. A horizontal rod held the fabric out; that is why the flag looks as though it is flying.

What all of these have in common is an odd arithmetic. One unexplained detail counts as proof; a mountain of ordinary evidence counts as nothing. For centuries the moon was associated with madness and with evil, and now it is associated with conspiracy instead. The story changes; the shape of the reasoning does not. A cheerful belief and a depressing one turn out to be equally difficult to remove, which suggests that what people are defending is not the claim itself but the pleasure of having noticed something everybody else has missed.

25.title: Inventive Ideas
25.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The net that drinks fog

An award-winning design on a Moroccan mountain — and why the clever part is not the technology.

🌌💧
1 · Before you read. A village in a dry region gets running water for the first time. Which change would you expect to matter most?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · How the water is caught

Written for this course, from the Wasserstiftung project reports on Mount Boutmezguida and Dar Si Hmad’s project documentation.

On Mount Boutmezguida, in the Anti-Atlas range of southwest Morocco, thick fog is pushed inland from the Atlantic on most mornings for about six months of the year. The mountain stands at 1,225 metres and receives well under 150 millimetres of rain in an average year. The phenomenon had been described for decades and was used by nobody. Today the moisture is caught in nets on the ridge, and the water is piped more than twenty kilometres down to villages where, until 2015, every litre had been carried up by hand or bought from a tanker.

The design is almost embarrassingly simple. Panels of mesh are attached to steel frames along the ridge; fog is driven through them by the wind; droplets condense on the threads, run down into a gutter and are stored in cisterns below. Nothing is burnt. No electricity is generated or consumed by the collection itself. On a foggy day the installation now yields around 37,000 litres, and the whole system was built without a single moving part.

Getting it to survive was the hard bit. Earlier fog nets in the region were repeatedly destroyed by the wind, and the more efficient the mesh was made, the more damaging that wind became. The version now in use, developed over more than two years by a German industrial designer working for a water foundation in Munich, is held by tensioners and shock cords and is rated to withstand gusts of 120 kilometres an hour. It was also designed to be repaired by the people who use it: residents are trained on site, and the installation is run by the community rather than by a contractor.

Text B · What the water changed

Written for this course, from the UNFCCC Momentum for Change citation (2016) and Dar Si Hmad’s project documentation.

The effect on the villages has been remarkable, and it is not mainly an effect on health. In a region where drought is normal, whether the fog arrives affects the shape of the whole day. Water had been fetched from distant wells by women and girls, who lost up to four hours of every day to the walk. Those hours were returned overnight. Girls who had been kept out of school by the journey were sent back to it; the time released was spent on argan oil and on paid work. When the project was recognised by the United Nations in 2016, it was honoured under a category for women’s-leadership results rather than for engineering.

The scale is modest and is usually overstated by people who write about it. Fewer than a hundred and fifty households were connected in the first phase. Fog harvesting works only where fog, altitude, terrain and community support happen to line up, and it is not offered by its own engineers as a general answer to water scarcity. What is striking is how much was achieved by a technology that could have been built in 1950.

Perhaps that is the point. An invention is usually called innovative when it is complicated, and this one was praised for inventiveness of exactly the opposite kind: a functional object with no pump, no fuel and nothing to break, kept working by the households it supplies. The technology is impressive but old. What was actually designed here was the arrangement around it — the training, the ownership and the repairs — and that is the part which is hardest to copy somewhere else.

26.title: Creative Environments
26.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

Three rooms people had built for thinking in

What designers actually change about their own workspaces — and why it is usually the opposite of what the brochures promise.

🎨🪑
1 · Before you read. A company knocks down the internal walls of its office. What happens to the amount of talking?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against paragraph 1.

Text A · Three rooms, three sets of changes

Written for this course. The three profiles are composites.

Anna, in Rotterdam, had the original open floor divided into four the year she took over, and has since had two more walls put in. She also had a ping-pong table placed in the middle of the largest room. Twenty minutes of mindless play, she says, sparks more than an afternoon of meetings ever has. The desks were specially built to be raised by hand, because she wanted people to stand up without asking anybody first, and she had the booking system rewritten twice until it was user-friendly enough that nobody came to her about it.

Tomas works above a shop in Ljubljana. He got the lamp posts outside the door yarn-bombed by a local knitting group, which cost him a week of arguments with the city and one afternoon of wool. The lights in the yard run on wind power from a turbine he had attached to the roof by an electrician. None of this is decoration, he insists: everything had to be practical first, and the wool is there because the street was grey and nobody was going to have it repainted for him.

Kiro, in Lagos, has had a slide built from the studio down to the lobby, and admits that it is a perk rather than a working condition — original, photogenic, and used about twice a week. What he defends is the room next to it, where a twenty-minute nap is treated as work rather than as time off. He gets his whole team sent outside at four to recharge, and a swing on the balcony is used by whoever gets there first. Friday afternoons off are a treat, he says. The nap room is not.

Text B · Why the pattern is the opposite of the brochure

Written for this course, from Bernstein & Turban, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 373:20170239 (2018).

The standard argument for the open office is that removing walls makes people talk to each other. In 2018 two researchers tested it properly, tracking employees at two corporate headquarters with wearable sensors and message logs before and after the walls came down. Face-to-face interaction fell by roughly seventy per cent in both cases, and email and instant messaging rose to replace it. People who could be seen at all times withdrew.

Read against that finding, the three rooms have something in common that none of their owners mentions. Not one of them had the space designed for them in advance. Every change was made after watching the room fail at something: Anna had the walls put back because nobody was concentrating, Tomas had the turbine fitted because the yard was unusable after dark, Kiro had the nap room built because his team were sleeping badly and lying about it. None of them got a consultant in first; each of them had the answer built after the problem had appeared. The slide was the exception, and it is the one he defends least.

That pattern fits the research better than the brochures do. An open plan is designed for an imagined worker who becomes more sociable when observed; the evidence says the opposite happens. A company that has its walls taken out to encourage conversation usually gets the conversation moved onto a screen instead. What these three had done, in their different ways, was put boundaries back — a wall, a door, a room with one clear purpose — and then defend them against the argument that a workplace should look open. It is a less impressive photograph than a slide, and it is harder to have copied, because what has to be copied is the noticing rather than the object. It is probably why the rooms work.

29.title: The Internet of Things
29.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The house that talks to itself

Fourteen connected devices in an average home, and the one night in 2016 that showed what they add up to.

🏠📶
1 · Before you read. Which of these worries you most about a smart device in your home?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · The night the sites went dark

Written for this course, from reporting on the October 2016 attack on Dyn and the UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022.

The phrase “internet of things” describes something very ordinary: objects which contain a small computer and a wireless connection. A smoke detector that tells you which room is on fire is one. So is a smart meter, which reports your electricity use without anybody reading a dial. None of this is new technology. What changed was the price, and a house with high-speed broadband now carries around fourteen internet-connected devices, most of which its owners could not list.

The technical problems that worried engineers in the 1990s were solved years ago. The ones that matter now are about who can access what, and the clearest demonstration came on 21 October 2016. Users across the United States found that Twitter, Netflix and Reddit had become unreachable, for hours. The cause was not a hostile government. It was a flood of traffic aimed at Dyn, a company which ran part of the internet’s address system, and the flood was produced by ordinary household objects.

The software behind it, which was named Mirai after a cartoon, was not sophisticated. It simply worked through a short list of about sixty usernames and passwords — the ones that cameras, routers and recorders are sold with — and tried them on every device it could find. A camera that can be hacked from the street is worse than no camera at all, and hundreds of thousands of machines whose owners had never changed a password were quietly recruited. Anyone whose baby monitor took part in that attack is still unaware of it. The code was published online, and variants of it are still responsible for a measurable share of attacks today.

Text B · The risk that no password fixes

Written for this course.

Governments have been slow, and then sudden. In April 2024 the United Kingdom became the first country to ban universal default passwords on consumer devices that connect to the internet. The law, which covers everything from doorbells to fridges, also requires manufacturers to publish a contact point for anybody who finds a fault, and it carries fines of up to ten million pounds. It is a small rule that addresses a large share of the problem, which tells you how basic the problem was. Manufacturers had known about the weakness for years and almost none of them had acted, because a device that is cheap to make and quick to install sells better than one that is difficult to break into.

The interesting risk, though, is duller than a botnet. The data any single device sends is trivial: a kettle boiled at 6.40, a light switched off at 23.10, a doorbell that nobody answered on Thursday. Put together, those readings describe a life — when the house is empty, who sleeps badly, whether anybody is ill. That pattern, which nobody ever agreed to hand over, is what the argument about privacy is actually about, and no password will fix it, because nothing in it was stolen.

Which may explain a small oddity. The users who are most tech-savvy, who understand exactly how little each individual reading contains, are often the ones with the fewest smart devices installed at home. They are not worried about being watched. They are worried about being described. Everybody else is told that the technology is convenient, which it is, and left to discover the rest — usually years later, and usually from somebody who is trying to sell them something.

30.title: Gen X, Gen Y, Gen Z
30.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

Three letters and very little evidence

Everybody knows what Gen X, Y and Z are like. Twenty thousand survey responses suggest otherwise.

👥📊
1 · Before you read. How different do you expect people born twenty years apart to be at work?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · What everybody knows

Written for this course.

Everybody knows the descriptions. Born between 1965 and 1980, Gen X are easy-going, family-focused and deeply suspicious of employers. Gen Y are fussy about who they work for, enthusiastic about the work itself and unimpressed by job titles. Gen Z, arriving last, are said to be either the most rebellious cohort in decades or the most conventional, depending on which article you happen to be reading; keen on stable jobs, optimistic about their own lives and pessimistic about everything else, they are described in terms that are supposed to be characteristic of a generation raised online. Asked to describe themselves, members of all three groups reach for the same words: open-minded, realistic, hard-working. Asked about the group below them, they become noticeably less generous, producing self-centred and arrogant within about a minute.

There is a labelling problem underneath all of this. Described by a manager who is sympathetic towards them, a young employee asking for feedback is self-confident; described by one who is not, the same employee is arrogant. Keen on flexible hours, they are either realistic about modern life or not loyal enough, and which of those you write down says more about you than about them.

We associate impatience with the young because we stop noticing it in ourselves, and the same answer, given by a twenty-year-old, is coded differently from the way it is coded when a fifty-year-old gives it. None of this is deliberate. It is what happens when a category is available and a judgement has to be made quickly, and it is the reason the descriptions in the first paragraph feel so obviously true to almost everybody who reads them.

Text B · What the evidence shows

Written for this course, from Costanza, Badger, Fraser, Severt & Gade, Journal of Business and Psychology 27(4), 2012.

Being confident about something is not the same as being right about it. In 2012 a team of researchers collected twenty published and unpublished studies covering nearly twenty thousand employees, comparing four generations on three things that organisations actually care about: job satisfaction, commitment to the employer, and intention to leave. Combining the studies statistically, they found differences that were small to moderate and, in many of the comparisons, essentially zero. Their conclusion was blunt: meaningful generational differences in these attitudes probably do not exist.

Understanding why the belief survives means separating three things that a single survey cannot separate. The first is age: people are different at twenty-five from how they are at fifty, whatever year they were born. The second is period — a recession or a housing crisis hits everybody at once, regardless of cohort. The third is generation proper. Run a survey in one year and all three arrive tangled together, and the tidiest explanation is usually the one that gets printed. The categories are also commercially useful, which is a different thing from being accurate: a birth year is easier to sell than a personality, and, having been repeated for thirty years, the labels now feel like observations rather than inventions.

What survives the criticism is modest but real. Shared events do shape people, and somebody who left university in 2009 entered a labour market that somebody leaving in 2006 never saw. But the boundaries are arbitrary — December 1980 and January 1981 are not two different worlds — and the variation inside any generation is far larger than the gap between them. Taken seriously, the research does not say that people are all alike. It says the dividing line is almost certainly not the year of birth.

33.title: As If It Were Yesterday
33.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The kitchen with the yellow door

One vivid childhood memory, one box of photographs, and what the research says about being certain.

🚪📸
1 · Before you read. How reliable do you think your own earliest memory is?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · The door was green

Written for this course.

I can recall it very clearly. I am four, sitting under the table in my grandmother’s kitchen, and the door to the yard is yellow. She is cutting something on the board above me and the radio keeps stopping. I remember hearing her laugh at whatever the radio said, and I remember deciding not to come out.

For thirty years I enjoyed telling that story. It is a vivid memory, one of maybe six that survive from my childhood, and vivid memories feel reliable, so I never bothered to check it. It was one of the few things I could offer when people asked about my childhood, and I told it the same way every time, which I now understand is exactly the problem: each telling was a copy of the last one rather than a return to the kitchen. Then last spring my aunt began sorting through the photographs, and I stopped believing my own account within about a minute.

The door was green. It had always been green, and it was painted yellow in 1998, when I was twenty-two. My aunt has no recollection of any radio in that kitchen; my mother vaguely remembers one, but in the other house. I just about remember the yard and have no memory whatsoever of the room beside it; shown the photographs, I managed to identify the table at once and nothing else. What everybody agrees on is that table, and the fact that I refused to come out from under it. Nobody in the family has tried to persuade me that the rest of it happened, which I notice I would have preferred.

Text B · Certain, and wrong

Written for this course, from Talarico & Rubin, Psychological Science 14(5), 2003.

None of this makes me unusual, and the tidiest evidence for that comes from a study that had nothing to do with kitchens. On 12 September 2001, fifty-four students at an American university were asked to write down what they remembered of hearing the previous day’s news, and also what they remembered of an ordinary event from the same week. They were tested again up to thirty-two weeks later. Both sets of memories lost consistent details at the same rate and picked up inconsistent ones at the same rate. Dramatic memories were not more accurate.

What did differ was confidence. Ratings of vividness, of recollection and of belief in one’s own accuracy declined for the everyday memories and stayed high for the dramatic ones. The students went on being certain about the memory that was decaying exactly as fast as the one they had stopped trusting, and most of them would have refused to accept that their own account had changed at all. The researchers put it plainly: such memories are not special in their accuracy, only in their perceived accuracy. That is a slightly frightening sentence, because it removes the one test most of us use.

I have stopped claiming the yellow door and I still see it. That is the part that unsettles me: knowing a detail is invented does not make it disappear. Psychologists will tell you that a memory has begun to fade the first time it is recalled, that memories are rebuilt rather than replayed, that the brain prefers to invent a plausible detail rather than to leave a gap, and that a photograph reminds you of the last telling rather than of the day. I believe them. I would just like to remember that kitchen once without the door.
