35.title: Come Up With It
35.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The shop that fixes things

One evening in Amsterdam in 2009, and what happened to the idea afterwards.

🔧☕
1 · Before you read. Your kettle stops working. What do you actually do?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · One afternoon in Amsterdam

Written for this course, from the Repair Café International Foundation’s published account of its own history.

The idea did not come up in a laboratory. In 2009 a Dutch journalist called Martine Postma, who had been writing about sustainability and had noticed how much her neighbours were throwing away, came up with something specific: one afternoon, one hall, free coffee, and volunteers who could hold a screwdriver. The first Repair Café was held in Amsterdam on 18 October 2009. She was not sure anybody would turn up. Instead, people arrived early, carrying appliances, clothes, furniture and, in at least one case, a musical instrument.

What happened next was not planned either. So many groups wanted to do the same thing that a foundation was set up in March 2010 simply to answer them, and it began producing manuals, posters and a starter kit so that nobody had to work out the format from scratch. Consequently, similar shops popped up in one country after another. By 2016 there were more than a thousand registered; today the figure has passed three thousand. Admittedly, that is still small against the scale of what gets discarded — but it grew without advertising, which is unusual.

The foundation has also tried to sort out a problem the volunteers created themselves. Every session generates knowledge — which brands fail, which faults recur, which parts cannot be bought — and for years all of it stayed in people’s heads. In 2017, therefore, an online tool was launched so that groups could record what each repair turned out to involve. Moreover, the records made it possible to compare one town with another. In other words, a movement built on Saturday afternoons quietly began to carry out research.

Text B · What a Saturday actually looks like

Written for this course. The town described here is a composite of several such groups.

In practice, a session looks less impressive than the numbers. In one English town that started a group after a public meeting, nineteen people turned up on the first Saturday, most of them over sixty, and they repaired forty-one things before lunch. Nobody had to make up a reason for coming. A lamp is not a symbol of anything; it is a lamp, and it either works afterwards or it does not.

The economics are what persuade councils, however, rather than the sentiment. A repair typically costs a fraction of a replacement, and volunteers find out very quickly that a surprising share of dead appliances have one cheap broken part. Nevertheless, nobody pretends the saving is large in itself. Therefore the case for the shop tends to be financial before it is ever environmental. In that town the funding ran out in the second winter, and yet the group stayed open, staffed by eleven volunteers and one paid hour a week.

None of which has fixed the underlying problem. Manufacturers still design products that are difficult to open, and several countries are only now beginning to phase out the rules that allowed it. Even so, the interesting part of the story is not the tools or the money. What turned out to matter was that somebody organised an afternoon and other people came. That is the least repeatable part of it, and it is the only part the starter kit cannot explain, which is presumably why the foundation spends so much of its time answering the same question from towns that already have everything else they need.

37.title: Extreme Streaming
37.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

Four in five of us say we do it

What binge-watching does to sleep, and why the number of hours turns out to be the wrong measurement.

📺😴
1 · Before you read. Which do you think matters more for how you sleep afterwards?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · What the study measured

Written for this course, from Exelmans & Van den Bulck, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 13(8), 2017.

In 2017 two researchers at a Belgian university asked four hundred and twenty-three adults between eighteen and twenty-five how they watched television. More than four in five described themselves as binge viewers — people who watch several episodes of the same drama series back to back — and, of those, about a fifth said that they had done it at least a few times a week in the previous month. Nobody at that point had asked whether the habit did any harm, and nobody had suggested that it might.

The answer was not the obvious one. The researchers reported that binge viewers had poorer sleep quality, more fatigue and more symptoms of insomnia than other people, and that binge viewers were roughly twice as likely to sleep badly. What makes the result interesting is the comparison. Ordinary television viewing — switching between a cookery programme with its celebrity chef, a home improvement programme with its DIY tips, whatever is on — showed no such link at all. Hours in front of a screen were not the problem.

What explained the difference was arousal. The study found that the effect ran entirely through how mentally alert people were as they went to bed: the mind stayed inside the story after the screen had been turned off. The lead author explained that the more often young people binge-watched, the higher their cognitive arousal before sleep, and said that this in turn affected sleep quality, fatigue and insomnia. She was careful about the limits, adding that the study was a survey rather than an experiment, so it could not establish which came first.

Text B · What the design does

Written for this course.

None of this is accidental on the producers’ side. A drama series is built with a gripping plot broken off at the worst possible moment and the next episode starting by itself, and no commercial break has ever survived contact with that design. Streaming did not invent the cliffhanger; it removed the week that used to follow it. Producers rarely deny this; one has said that the aim is simply to remove every reason to stop, and another has admitted that the design works best on tired people. When a colleague asked me what had actually changed since the days of one episode a week, the honest answer was: the pause.

There is a gap, too, between what people say they watch and what they finish. Asked what they would like more of, viewers almost always mention a current affairs programme or in-depth news, and the same viewers spend the evening with an old sitcom they have already seen twice, playing while they do something else. That is not dishonesty. It is the difference between the viewer somebody intends to be and the one who is tired at half past ten.

The authors’ own recommendation is duller than the headlines it produced. They argued that measures of media exposure ought to take account of how engaged the user is, not merely how long the screen was on, and suggested that anything which reduces arousal before bed would help more than a rule about hours. Whether a habit is addictive, in other words, may depend less on how much of it you consume than on how far into it you go — which is an uncomfortable thought, because engagement is exactly what everybody says they want from television.

39.title: Untangling Complex Sentences
39.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

Sixty-nine days underground

Long sentences, on purpose. The rescue everybody remembers, and the decade nobody reported.

⛏️🚦
1 · Before you read. A famous rescue is retold for years. Which part of the story usually gets left out?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · Before the drill arrived

Written for this course, from the Encyclopaedia Britannica account of the 2010 Chile mine rescue and contemporary reporting.

The San José copper and gold mine, which lies in the Atacama Desert some forty-five kilometres north of Copiapó and which had killed eight workers between 1998 and 2010, was closed in July 2010 after a rock fall cost a miner his leg, was allowed to reopen on the twenty-eighth of that month once corrective measures had been reported — an economic decision as much as a technical one — and collapsed one week later — a sequence that is almost never mentioned in the accounts which made the rescue famous, and which is treated, in most of them, as historical background rather than as the most relevant thing on the page.

When the main ramp closed at two in the afternoon on 5 August, trapping thirty-three men at a depth of seven hundred metres and five kilometres from the entrance, the group made for the ventilation shafts, which existed precisely so that men could climb out of a blocked mine and which should therefore have settled the matter in an hour; but the ladders required by the safety code were not there, and the men, having found the one route the regulations promised them and having found it unusable, went back down to the refuge to wait.

For seventeen days nobody above ground knew whether they were alive, and survival in that period depended not on the drilling equipment, which was still being assembled, but on the men themselves, who rationed two days of emergency food across a fortnight and organised, without being asked to, the shifts and the sleeping arrangements that a psychologist would later describe as the reason the mental strain never became unmanageable. Several exploratory boreholes missed the chamber entirely, the mine’s own maps having proved less reliable than anyone expected; the eighth found it, and came back up with a note attached.

Text B · Where the telling begins

Written for this course, from contemporary reporting on the rescue and its aftermath.

What followed was impressive by any objective measure: three separate drilling plans running at once, of which the one that broke through was a rig normally used for boring water holes rather than for reaching people; a medical team on site well before the shaft was finished; and, on 13 October, an operation lasting about twenty-two hours which brought every one of the thirty-three to the surface and which an estimated one billion people watched.

What followed was also, in the way it was told, extremely selective, because the account that reached that billion began on the day the drill arrived rather than in the decade when the warnings were ignored, and a story that begins in the right place is inspiring in a way that a story beginning in the wrong one never is. A congressional commission afterwards placed the blame on the mine’s owners and on the state body that was supposed to inspect them, which is a sentence that appeared in far fewer places than the pictures did.

The ending is less tidy than the broadcast. Many of the men were left with lasting physical and mental difficulties, several were unable to work, and the compensation they were awarded — upheld by Chile’s Supreme Court in 2023, at about forty-eight thousand dollars each for the thirty-one who took part in the case — arrived thirteen years after the collapse. It is an unfortunate fact about rescues that the part which is easy to film is also the part that ends, while the medical and economic consequences, which have no obvious final image, continue long after the cameras have been packed away.

41.title: Can You Believe Your Eyes?
41.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The photograph that split the internet

One badly lit picture, thirteen thousand people, and what your eyes are actually doing.

👀👗
1 · Before you read. When two people describe the same thing differently, what do you usually assume?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · A bad photograph, described

Written for this course, from Lafer-Sousa, Hermann & Conway, Current Biology 25(13), 2015.

It is not a good photograph. A small, badly lit, slightly blurred image of a dress on a hanger, taken at a wedding in Scotland and posted online in February 2015, it is overexposed at the top, where the window is, and murky at the bottom. The fabric is smooth and heavy; the lace running down it has a sharp repeating pattern; and the light source, which is the whole problem, is not visible in the frame at all.

Within a day, several million people were arguing about it. Some observed a long, pale white dress with dull gold lace. Others saw a dark blue dress with hard black lace and could not understand what anybody else was talking about. Households divided. People sent the picture to each other expecting agreement and got a fight. The illusion was not that one group was careless; both groups were looking hard, and each could describe in detail what the other was failing to see.

Two facts settled quickly. The real garment is blue and black — that can be checked, and it was. And a group of American researchers, publishing within months, used the word “striking” in their title for the individual differences the photograph revealed, which is unusual language for a scientific paper and tells you how odd the result seemed to people who study vision for a living. Normal, healthy vision was producing two incompatible answers from one small rectangle of colour, and no eye test in existence would have told you which answer a given person was about to give, because nothing was wrong with anybody’s eyes.

Text B · What your brain subtracts

Written for this course, from Wallisch, Journal of Vision 17(4), 2017.

The explanation arrived in 2017, from a survey of more than thirteen thousand people. The question that mattered was not about colour at all: it was what viewers assumed about the light. Four out of five of those who thought the dress had been photographed in shadow saw it as white and gold, because a brain that assumes cool blue daylight subtracts blue and leaves warm colours behind. Anybody who assumed ordinary yellow indoor lighting subtracted yellow instead, and was left with blue and black — which is what the dress is.

Then came the strange part. The researcher asked participants when they got up, and found that early risers, who spend their waking hours under a bright blue sky, were significantly more likely to see white and gold, while night owls, whose long evenings are spent under warm artificial light, tended to see blue and black. A lifetime of ordinary illumination had quietly set the assumption. Age and sex mattered far less.

What this reveals is that vision is not a recording. Your eyes receive light that has reflected off an object, and the object’s colour and the colour of the lamp arrive mixed together; the brain has to remove one to report the other, and it does this constantly and without asking. It is the same machinery that tells you a half-submerged wooden oar is straight rather than bent, that a solid white shirt is still white at sunset, and that one twinkling orange light on dark water is a single lamp rather than twenty. Almost always it is right. On one overexposed photograph it was not, and for once you could spot the working.

42.title: Sense of Humour
42.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The world’s funniest joke was nobody’s favourite

Two million ratings, seventy countries, and what actually stops a joke crossing a border.

😂🌐
1 · Before you read. When a comedy from another country does not make you laugh, what is usually missing?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · Two million ratings

Written for this course, from the LaughLab experiment run by the psychologist Richard Wiseman with the British Association for the Advancement of Science, 2001–2002.

In 2001 a British psychologist put a website online and invited the world to submit jokes and rate other people’s. Over the following year he collected around forty thousand jokes and close to two million ratings from more than seventy countries, each rating given on a five-point scale that the project called, inevitably, the Giggleometer. It remains one of the largest experiments on humour ever attempted.

The winner was a short, well-built joke about two hunters, one of whom misunderstands an emergency operator with fatal results. It is neat rather than hilarious, and the researcher was honest about why it won: it did not top anybody’s personal list, but almost nobody rated it distasteful. A joke can win a worldwide vote provided that it offends no one, which is a different achievement from being funny; and if a joke has to please seventy countries at once, it will not be anybody’s favourite even if it is everybody’s second choice. Unless a competition is designed to reward strong reactions, it will reward inoffensiveness instead.

The national patterns were more interesting than the winner. Raters in Britain, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand tended to prefer wordplay — a witty final line that turns on a double meaning. Americans and Canadians more often chose jokes in which one person is made to look ridiculous by another. Several continental European groups favoured the surreal, and jokes about illness and death that other raters found faintly distasteful. Germans, who are routinely accused of having no sense of humour at all, gave high ratings across the widest range of joke types of anyone in the study. These are tendencies rather than rules: a preference only counts as a pattern if thousands of people share it, and even if they do, plenty of individuals inside every group will disagree.

Text B · The rule you have to know already

Written for this course.

None of that describes a nation, and it would be irritating to pretend otherwise. Anybody who volunteers to spend an evening rating jokes on a website in 2001 is, by definition, an unusual person, and the sample selected itself. Unless you can draw people at random, you are describing the visitors to one website rather than a country. The finding is real as long as it is stated that carefully, and pointless the moment somebody turns it into a claim about national character.

What the experiment could not measure is the thing that actually stops comedy at borders. A joke is not funny unless you know which rule is being broken, and the rule is usually local. A long silence is hilarious in a country where people do not interrupt each other, and merely tedious where they do. A character who cannot say what he means is comical to one audience and simply annoying to another, which keeps waiting for a punchline that the writers never intended to supply, and which comes away finding the whole performance predictable rather than thought-provoking.

Some things travel anyway. Physical comedy survives almost everywhere, as long as the situation is clear within about five seconds. So does the absurd, provided that it is played completely straight: a ridiculous premise performed by actors behaving as though it were entirely normal seems to work on every audience anybody has tried it on. What does not survive is anything built on a specific social rule, unless the viewer already holds it, and no amount of subtitling will install it. The remakes that succeed keep the shape and rewrite the rule; the ones that fail translate the rule faithfully, protect every line of the original, and then wonder why the room is quiet.

45.title: Nearest and Dearest
45.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The families we did not have

Everyone knows what their brothers and sisters did to them. Twenty thousand people suggest otherwise.

👪💭
1 · Before you read. How much do you think your position in the family shaped your character?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · Four familiar answers

Written for this course. The four speakers are composites, not interviews.

Ask people about family size and you will hear principles. Ask them about their own childhood and you will hear something more useful. Here are four familiar kinds of answer, and one problem with all of them.

The only child says she was never spoilt, which everybody with a sibling assumes she was, and that her godparent took her more seriously than either grandmother did, as did a second cousin she still writes to. If she had had a brother, she says, she would have learnt earlier how to stand up to bullies; as it was, she learnt it at twenty-three, in an office. She would not change it. She would simply have liked one person to be mean to her at the right age.

The third of four describes years of feeling left out and mentions it once, in passing, as though it were a weather report. His older brother told him off more often than his parents ever did. If his mother had not become ill, he thinks, he would still not be speaking to that brother; somebody had to care for her, they both moved home, and the relationship changed in a single winter. He is now devoted to a brother he did not speak to for six years. The mother of four calls it a blessing and a travelling circus, and says the joy each one brings is immeasurable and the strain enormous. The fourth speaker, who has no children, is the one who spots the pattern: everybody defends the family they have. If she had had children, she says, she would be defending them now, and she would be just as certain as everyone else in the room, and she would have no more evidence than they do.

Text B · Twenty thousand adults

Written for this course, from Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle, PNAS 112(46), 2015, and Falbo & Polit, Psychological Bulletin 100(2), 1986.

The fourth speaker is closer to the research than the others. In 2015 three psychologists combined data from three national panels — more than twenty thousand adults in Germany, the United States and Britain — to test the oldest folk theory in the field: that your position among your brothers and sisters shapes the person you become. They confirmed one small effect. Firstborns score slightly higher on measured intelligence, and rate their own intellect slightly higher too. If the effect had been any larger, somebody would have found it decades ago.

On personality they found nothing. No birth-order effect on how outgoing people were, how emotionally stable, how agreeable, how conscientious, how imaginative. The differences everybody can describe from their own kitchen, in detail, with examples, did not appear in twenty thousand people. The only child fares no worse either: a review of the research had already concluded that only children do as well as anybody else, and better on some measures, which will disappoint several centuries of confident opinion about them. If the study had confirmed what everybody expected, it would have been reported everywhere; as it was, the null result had to be argued for.

What all this leaves is a strange situation. The sentences people use about their families are almost all counterfactual — if I had had a sister, if he had not been born first, if she had not been the youngest — and a counterfactual cannot be checked, because the other family was never run. Nobody grew up twice. That is not a reason to stop saying them, and the four speakers are not being foolish. It is a reason to notice that such a sentence describes a feeling accurately and a cause not at all.

46.title: If I Could Turn Back Time
46.html:
Stage 3 · Reading

The regret nobody puts on the form

Eleven studies, one ranking, and a rule about where regret goes that explains the whole list.

⌛📜
1 · Before you read. Which do you think people regret more, looking back over a whole life?

Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Text A · The list and the reason for it

Written for this course, from Roese & Summerville, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 31(9), 2005.

In 2005 two psychologists gathered eleven separate studies in which people had been asked to rank their biggest regrets, and combined them. The result was a list. In descending order: education, career, romance, parenting, the self, leisure. What is missing from the top of that list is as interesting as what is on it. Almost nobody wishes they had started a private pension earlier, which surprises the people who commission surveys and nobody else. If only I had saved more is a sentence almost no one says without prompting.

The researchers then explained the ranking with a single idea. Regret concentrates wherever people see the most opportunity. Education comes first not because school is the most important thing that happens to anybody, but because it feels like the most open door: there is always another course, another qualification, another year you could have used. Where a door is genuinely shut, regret is quieter. That is why the list looks the way it does, and it is a more useful finding than the list itself.

A second pattern comes from earlier work on the difference between doing something and failing to do it. In the short term, people regret their actions — the thing they said, the job they turned down, the message they sent at one in the morning. Over years, the balance reverses, and what people regret is inaction: the course not applied for, the conversation not had, the opportunity they missed out on without recognising it as one at the time, because it looked like a coincidence rather than a choice. Ask people at seventy and they wish they had tried; ask them at thirty and they wish they had said less.

Text B · What the sentences sound like

Written for this course. The individuals described are composites.

You can hear the difference in how the two kinds of regret are phrased. A regretted action has edges. A man who turned down a job offer in 2011 can tell you the date, the room and the salary, and he has been explaining it to himself ever since; what he says he regrets is not the refusal but the six months he spent not deciding. A regretted inaction has no edges at all, which is exactly why it lasts: there is no single moment to point at, so it never finishes being thought about.

The third pattern is slower and harder to put on a form. People wish they had got to grips earlier with what they actually wanted, and they describe ambitions that had not switched but evolved, quietly, while they were busy defending an older version of themselves. If only somebody had told me, they say; and, when pressed, most admit that somebody had.

Romance sits third on the published list, and it is where the phrasing gets simplest. People wish they had turned to the right person sooner, and made up after the row years earlier than they did. One woman had not spoken to her brother for eleven years, and they made it up in a car park; she wishes it had been a car park in 2014. Nobody says quality time without embarrassment, but it is what they mean, and several call the cost immeasurable — which is the word people reach for once they have counted. If only, they say, and then they give you the year, which rather suggests they have known it all along.
